# Functions & prep

```{r}
# all sheets into a list. I can then call the df directly from the list rather than making extra dfs all over the place
df_list <- excel_sheets("A3_20001249.xlsx") %>%
  set_names() %>%
  map(read_excel, path = "A3_20001249.xlsx")

liking <- unlist(df_list$Liking[2])
```


```{r long format df}
#making a long format dataframe for EDA with liking. This way things are going to be more simple to work with
EDA_df <- cbind(df_list$Flavour) %>% pivot_longer(cols = -1, values_to = 'Score', names_to = 'Characteristic') %>% mutate(Measure = 'Flavour') %>%
  rbind(
    cbind(df_list$Taste) %>% pivot_longer(cols = -1, values_to = 'Score', names_to = 'Characteristic') %>% mutate(Measure = 'Taste') 
  ) %>%
  rbind(
    cbind(df_list$Texture) %>% pivot_longer(cols = -1, values_to = 'Score', names_to = 'Characteristic') %>% mutate(Measure = 'Texture') 
    ) %>%
  left_join(df_list$Liking, by = 'insect') %>%
  #adding in some extra columns for EDA
  group_by(Characteristic) %>%
  mutate(Score_diff_from_mean = Score - mean(Score), mean_score = mean(Score)) %>% ungroup()
```

```{r flavour summary table and corrplot function, warning=FALSE}
summary_eda <- function(df, sheet) {
  table <-broom::tidy(df_list[[sheet]][-1]) %>% knitr::kable()
  print(table)
  #I am going to do some code you probably won't like, because I am nesting functions within functions. I am doing this to avoid flooding the namespace with unnecessary objects out of the EDA. 
  corrplot::corrplot(cor(cbind(df_list$Liking[-1], df_list[[sheet]][-1])), type = 'lower', 
                     title = paste("Correlation plot for", sheet), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
}
```

```{r EDA function, fig.width=15, fig.height=15}
eda_plots <- function(df, measure) {
  #----- Top layer------
  #column plot showing how many times a characteristic was the highest scored for an animal
  col_plot <- df %>% filter(Measure == measure) %>%
    group_by(insect) %>%                
    slice_max(order_by = Score, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% # Pick top score per group
    ungroup() %>%
    count(Characteristic, sort = TRUE) %>%
    ggplot(aes(y = Characteristic, x = n) ) + geom_col() +
    labs(title = paste('Top Scoring', measure, 'by Insect')) +
    theme_minimal()
  
  # see total score of characteristics for insects
  total_char <- df %>% filter(Measure == measure) %>%
    group_by(Characteristic) %>%
    summarise(total = sum(Score), liking = mean(liking), .groups = 'drop') %>% arrange(desc(total)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x=total, y = Characteristic, color = total)) + 
    geom_point(size = 2) + 
    geom_segment(aes(xend=0), linewidth = 1) +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = 'Total Scores by Characteristic', y = '') +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1), legend.position='none',  axis.text.y = element_blank())
  
  #---- bottom layer------
  #see which insect has the highest difference in overall score mean
  total_insects <- df %>% filter(Measure == measure) %>% 
    group_by(insect) %>%
    summarise(diff = mean(Score_diff_from_mean), .groups = 'drop') %>%
    mutate(insect = factor(insect, levels = unique(insect[order(diff, decreasing = FALSE)]))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x=diff, y = insect, color = diff)) + 
    geom_point() + 
    geom_segment(aes(xend=0)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, col = 'black', linetype = "dashed") + 
    scale_color_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1) + 
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = 'Insect Total Scores differnce from mean score', color = 'total difference', y = "") +
    theme(legend.position = 'bottom')
  
  #heatmap showing the worksheet by insect with likness score on right y axis. 
  heatmap <- df %>% filter(Measure == measure) %>% mutate(insect = factor(insect, levels = unique(insect[order(Score, decreasing = FALSE)]))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = Characteristic, y = insect, fill = Score)) +
      geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) + 
      scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1) + 
      theme_minimal() +
      theme(
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1), 
        panel.grid = element_blank()
       ) +
      labs(fill = "Score", title = paste("Insect", measure, "Scores"), x = "", y = "") +
      coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
      theme(plot.margin = margin(5.5, 40, 5.5, 5.5), legend.position = 'bottom') 
  
  (col_plot | total_char) / (heatmap | total_insects) + 
    plot_annotation(title = paste("Insect", measure, "EDA"),
                    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))
)
}

```

```{r}
pca_analysis <- function(data, y, n_plots, n_rotations) { #got to pass in the dataframe with insects dropped, and y = unlist(df_list$Liking[2])
  #1. do the PCA
  pca <- prcomp(data)
  
  #2. Scree plot. This is how I get n_plots and n_rotations. I ran this many times 
  fviz_screeplot(pca)
  
  #3 loop to get the bi-plots. I pretty much only show three each time though. It is too much to show many more and explain each one. 
  combos <- combn(1:n_plots, 2)
  
  for (i in 1:ncol(combos)) {
    x_axes = combos[1, i]
    y_axes =  combos[2, i]
    fviz_pca_biplot(pca, 
                repel = TRUE, 
                axes = c(x_axes, y_axes), 
                col.ind = y, 
                gradient.cols = c("#9F2F7FFF", "#FDE725FF", "#94D840FF"),
                title = paste("PCA Biplot PCs", x_axes, "and", y_axes)) + 
  coord_equal()
  }
  
  #another loop to get the rotation table. I am going to do it a bit strange. I want a table with PCs along the top, and each value is a tibble of characteristics and value. This way I can see each PC's rotation comparatively. 
  
}
```

```{r parallel coord plot for taste, fig.width=20, fig.height=8}

question_3 <- function(data, n) {
top_insects <- data$Liking %>% arrange(desc(liking)) %>% head(n) %>% select(insect)

  
P1 <- ggparcoord({data$Flavour %>% filter(insect %in% top_insects$insect)}, columns = 2:15, groupColumn = 1, showPoints = TRUE, alphaLines = 0.3, scale="globalminmax") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Insects Flavour Scores") +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

P2 <- ggparcoord({data$Taste %>% filter(insect %in% top_insects$insect)}, columns = 2:6, groupColumn = 1, showPoints = TRUE, alphaLines = 0.3, scale="globalminmax") +

  labs(title = "Insects Taste Scores") +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

P3 <- ggparcoord({data$Texture %>% filter(insect %in% top_insects$insect)}, columns = 2:6, groupColumn = 1, showPoints = TRUE, alphaLines = 0.3, scale="globalminmax") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Insects Texture Scores") +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

P1 / P2 / P3
}
```

Note, what is chemically sour vs what people call sour taste are different. People call tart or tangy flavours 'sour' as in a granny smith apple or a lemon curd or the loosely defined 'freshness' often described in vinegrettes. These are not 'sour' as such, but are mildly sour, braced by sweetness which humans like. 'Sour' which is the presence of chemical acids, is not an enjoyable experience for most people. Here, we cna see this misinterpretation in action.

### Q5 - Statistical models (25 marks)

#### Q5a - Flavour, Taste, or Texture?

*Discuss which of the three characteristics (Flavour, Taste, or Texture), if any, you now consider the most important. In your answer, consider your findings from your previous analyses as well as any other contextual (or otherwise) information.* 
Taste.
Taste is the biggest element to the success of a dish. As an ex-chef I know this very well. Aromas can be masked or changed by cooking. Texture can be likewise controlled to some extent. If worst comes to worst, puree it and go from there. Taste, which is also changeable, is the most important thing. 
This analysis is now somewhat moot. If you have this flavour profile data with texture and Flavour (which is mostly aroma), then you have a catalogue of ingredients a chef can use. Give a skilled chef these products and they can make something tasty. 
I know, I have cooked with some of these insects before.

### Q6 - Your Menu (15 marks)

*Design three (simple!) courses for your opening menu using bug-based food. Justify any decision made using your analysis and conclusions above. The three courses can be of any combination type (e.g., three starters, or one main and two desserts etc.), and should be constrained to those characteristics that you have information for (i.e., are in the survey).*

Insects (what we are calling this group of invertebrates, not all of which are insects), are small and annoying to work with to create main dishes. And they are costly to acquire and process, so you aren't likely to break even. Additionally, they are often difficult to make into dish 'stars' because they have lesser flavours than commonly available ingredients. Unless they are dehydrated to increase their potency, which is overkill because dehydrated bugs are flaky and dry out the mouth. All this points to the use of insects as seasoning or ingredients in other dishes. An example form a place I used to work at was Danish Orange ants served live on creme friache. The taste of a zingy orange was the pheromones of the ants panicking as they were eaten. This was considered novel at the time, and because they aren't cute, no one cares about animal cruelty directed at insects. Luckily this isn't an ethics paper!

Morio worm pate: having eaten witchetty grubs in Australia as a kid, and knowing that Morio worms are in fact a grub, I know from experience that the worst part about them is the exoskeleton. It can get stuck in your teeth. In this dish, the exoskeleton is blended into a fine pate. Many people enjoy a chicken or duck liver pate, but baulk at the unprocessed liver. The same concept is applied here. Make a boozy pate and serve with crusty bread. The benefit of this dish is that a pate's seasoning can be adjusted to achieve whatever flavour is desired, and so the buttery flavour of grubs can be complemented by spices or other accoutrements. 
Smoking the grubs over straw will help counter their less desirable traits. 

Termite crackers with taramasalata: Termites are not sour, mildly sweet, quite high bitter, salty and umami. That sounds like a toasted grain. Toasted rye or wheat berries, but with umami added. The idea in this dish is to puree the termites, mix them with a biding agent, spread them thin and dehydrate them into thin crackers that will be snapped into shards. These can be served with the taramasalata made from salted and cured cod roe. 

Duck a la lemon ant - live. In order to thicken sauces, one can use a protein that coagulates as it heats to thicken the sauce. Blood sauce is thickened this way, and using egg yolk or cream is another example of this. This dish is a play on Duck a la orange. The sauce is instead thickened with a puree of lemon ants. They need to be pureed alive in order to extract their delicious panic. Then the liquidated protein can be used to thicken and season the duck pan juices. We can then get some dried ants, mix them with pepper and season with a lemon ant pepper for presentation.

**BugB: mushroom, soft, salty.**
